purpose: Piperacillin is used to treat serious bacterial infections in different parts of the body, including the lungs, skin, urinary tract, abdomen, and blood. It is often used in hospital settings for infections that are harder to treat. Your doctor may combine it with another medicine called tazobactam to make it work even better against tough bacteria.
how_it_works: Piperacillin works by attacking the outer wall that surrounds bacteria. Think of that wall like a protective shell — piperacillin pokes holes in it and breaks it down, causing the bacteria to fall apart and die. Your body's immune system can then clear out the remaining bacteria more easily.
common_side_effects: Diarrhea or loose stools, nausea, vomiting, rash or itching, headache, pain or irritation at the injection site, and low potassium levels in your blood. Some people may notice their liver enzymes go up slightly, which your doctor will monitor.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you develop a severe rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or have trouble breathing — these could be signs of a serious allergic reaction. Let your doctor know if you have ever had an allergic reaction to penicillin or amoxicillin. This medication can sometimes cause a serious bowel infection called C. difficile, so tell your doctor if you get severe or persistent diarrhea. It can also affect your blood counts and kidney function, so routine lab tests may be needed.
typical_dosing: Piperacillin is given as an injection or IV (through a vein) in a hospital or clinic — it is not taken by mouth. The dose depends on the type and severity of your infection, your weight, and how well your kidneys are working. Adults typically receive doses every 4 to 6 hours. Your healthcare team will set the exact dose and schedule that is right for you.
